## Proof

**Claim:** Yes, such a δ > 0 exists.

**Setup.** Let $\{U_\alpha\}$ be an open cover of $S^{n-1}$, where $n \geq 2$. Since $S^{n-1}$ is a closed and bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$, it is **compact** (Heine–Borel). Being an open cover of a compact set, $\{U_\alpha\}$ admits a finite subcover: there exist indices $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m$ such that

$$S^{n-1} \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{m} U_{\alpha_i}.$$

**Defining the distance function.** For each $i = 1, \dots, m$, define the function $f_i : S^{n-1} \to \mathbb{R}$ by

$$f_i(x) = \operatorname{dist}(x,\, \mathbb{R}^n \setminus U_{\alpha_i}).$$

Since $U_{\alpha_i}$ is open, $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus U_{\alpha_i}$ is closed, so $f_i(x)$ is well-defined and continuous (the distance-to-a-closed-set function is Lipschitz). Moreover, $f_i(x) > 0$ if and only if $x \in U_{\alpha_i}$.

Now define $f : S^{n-1} \to \mathbb{R}$ by

$$f(x) = \max_{i=1,\dots,m} f_i(x).$$

As the maximum of finitely many continuous functions, $f$ is continuous. Since $\{U_{\alpha_1}, \dots, U_{\alpha_m}\}$ covers $S^{n-1}$, for every $x \in S^{n-1}$ there exists some $i$ with $x \in U_{\alpha_i}$, hence $f_i(x) > 0$, and therefore $f(x) > 0$.

**Using compactness.** The continuous function $f$ attains its minimum on the compact set $S^{n-1}$. Let

$$\delta_0 = \min_{x \in S^{n-1}} f(x) > 0.$$

(The inequality is strict because $f > 0$ everywhere on $S^{n-1}$.)

**The annulus is covered.** Set $\delta = \delta_0 / 2 > 0$. We claim

$$A_\delta := \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : 1 - \delta < \|x\| < 1 + \delta\} \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{m} U_{\alpha_i} \subseteq \bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha.$$

Take any $x \in A_\delta$ with $x \neq 0$ (note $\delta < 1$ since $S^{n-1}$ has radius $1$ and $f$ is bounded above by $1$ on the sphere, so $\delta_0 \leq 1$, giving $\delta \leq 1/2 < 1$; thus $1 - \delta > 0$ and $x \neq 0$). Let

$$y = \frac{x}{\|x\|} \in S^{n-1}.$$

Then $\|x - y\| = \big|\|x\| - 1\big| < \delta$.

By definition of $\delta_0 = \min_{S^{n-1}} f$, we have $f(y) \geq \delta_0$, so there exists $i \in \{1,\dots,m\}$ with $f_i(y) \geq \delta_0$, i.e.,

$$\operatorname{dist}(y,\, \mathbb{R}^n \setminus U_{\alpha_i}) \geq \delta_0.$$

This means the open ball $B(y, \delta_0) \subseteq U_{\alpha_i}$. Since $\|x - y\| < \delta = \delta_0/2 < \delta_0$, we conclude $x \in B(y, \delta_0) \subseteq U_{\alpha_i}$.

Therefore every $x \in A_\delta$ lies in some $U_{\alpha_i}$, proving $A_\delta \subseteq \bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha$.

**Conclusion.** There exists $\delta > 0$ (explicitly, $\delta = \tfrac{1}{2}\min_{x \in S^{n-1}} \max_i \operatorname{dist}(x, \mathbb{R}^n \setminus U_{\alpha_i})$, where $\{U_{\alpha_i}\}_{i=1}^m$ is any finite subcover) such that the annulus $\{x : 1-\delta < \|x\| < 1+\delta\}$ is covered by $\{U_\alpha\}$. $\blacksquare$
